issue.title: The energy price cap looks set to jump 27% in January
issue.question: Energy bills are forecast to rise sharply from January. Who should pay to cushion the rise: every household, only the poorest, or nobody?
issue.summary: Uswitch, using predictions from British Gas, EDF and E.ON Next as of 16 November 2026, puts the January 2027 price cap for a typical household at about £2,184 a year, about 27% above the current £1,723 cap. Ofgem is due to announce the real figure on or before 25 November, using wholesale prices from 19 August to 17 November. The new cap starts on 1 January 2027. Forecasts from September were lower, between £1,872 and £2,165, and none of them is official.
issue.slot_reason: Energy had not come up yet in the simulation, and the forecast rise in the price cap was in the UK news that day.

bench.title: Aim help at those who can't pay; fix the cap's debt rules
bench.answer: No cheque for every household. In 2022 that cost £36 billion (s4). Keep Ofgem and the suppliers, but change the rules. The Government would pay an automatic winter credit only to households on means-tested benefits, matched from tax and benefit records, with the council covering the old and sick who miss out. Ofgem would ban debt chasing and forced prepayment meters for them until spring. Fund it by taking the old policy costs off electricity bills, worth about £60 a year (s3), and by not cutting NHS, schools or councils. It worked if household energy debt stops climbing towards £7 billion (s4) and few eligible homes are missed.

bench.title: Set up a public energy arm to insulate homes and carry bills
bench.answer: Make a publicly owned energy body, run by a board that includes bill-payers chosen by lot. Its first job is a fast, free insulation drive. It starts with the homes of people who can't pay, and it works through councils. It also takes over help for people in arrears, so help is aimed at need, not paid to everyone. In 2022/23 universal support cost £36 billion (s4). Household energy debt may reach £7 billion by the end of 2026 (s4). We'd know it worked if debt stops growing, cap rises hurt poorer homes less, and the board publishes homes finished and money saved each quarter.

bench.title: Let households steer a local warmth fund
bench.answer: In this simulation, help goes to households that cannot afford enough heat. The January rise is still a forecast (s1). Parliament would fund local warmth funds through a levy on the richest households. Councils would handle payments, with elected service users setting priorities and checking spending. The funds would cover urgent bills and insulation for homes receiving help. Existing help for older and sick people would stay. NHS, school and council budgets would not fund it. Insulation firms would receive their final payment only after independent checks. After winter, success means fewer missed bills and fewer households reporting cold homes among those helped.

rows.note: Pays only households on means-tested benefits. Energy UK (s4) calls universal support inefficient and asks for targeted help.

gate.verdict: No answer clears every test and limit; C comes closest, with one test unclear. Facts can't settle whether to help the poorest only or lasting insulation first, or who should pay.

jury.question: With the January rise coming, should the money go first to quick help for households that can't pay, or to insulation that cuts bills for good, and who should pay?
options: Quick help now for households that can't pay, paid for by the richest
Insulation for good, starting with the poorest homes, even if it is slower
Quick help now, paid for through general taxation
jury.ruling: Quick help now for households that can't pay, paid for by the richest. Five of twelve chose it, because help is needed before January and the jurors did not want working people to pay.

reasons.text: Quick help for those struggling, paid by those with the most. Not by people who work for a living.
I've lived in cold flats. Fixing the walls and windows is the only help that lasts.
Winter is here and I'm on my own. Help now, through general tax so it's quick and simple.
Targeted help, paid by the richest, not the middle. Insulation can wait a little.

minister.trial: A winter credit for households on means-tested benefits in one region, paid before 1 January, funded by a levy on the richest households there. The council pays the old and sick who miss out and the same money starts insulation on their homes.
minister.fail_number: Fewer than 80% of eligible households in the trial region paid by 1 January, or the levy raises less than the credits cost.
minister.statement: Five of twelve jurors said help now, and make the richest pay for it. Not workers. Picture a pensioner with the heating off and the cap going up. So one region, one winter credit, paid before January. The council catches the old and sick who miss out. Insulation is slower, and the jury gave it less. We'll watch the number: how many get paid, and does the levy cover it.
